items.question: How does wheelchair fencing work?
items.answer: The chairs are fixed to frames, so fencers always stay at a set distance from each other and cannot tip out of the chair. The distance is set with the arm outstretched, touching the opponent's elbow with the tip of the weapon. Hits land quickly, especially in sabre, so you have to train your reflexes. It is great fun.

items.question: Can I train if I have no physical limitation?
items.answer: Of course, you can train with the rest of the group. We are always glad when standing fencers come and give it a try. To compete officially in this category, you do need an impairment that justifies using a wheelchair.

items.question: Are there categories within wheelchair fencing?
items.answer: Yes: category A (the impairment does not prevent movement of the lower body), category B (the lower body is affected but abdominal movement is kept) and category C (people who have lost abdominal strength, as in cases of tetraplegia).

items.question: Do I need to buy equipment?
items.answer: In your first month, you can use the club's equipment for free. From the second month you can buy your own, or rent the electrical equipment (electric jacket, mask and sabre) for {1} per item per month.

items.question: The sessions are in the morning. Can I come in the evening?
items.answer: If another fencer is able to train in the evening, we can open that up occasionally, as long as you let the available coaches know in advance.

items.question: Is there recreational wheelchair fencing?
items.answer: Yes, on exactly the same terms as in the Adults group.

items.question: Do I have to hold a federation licence?
items.answer: Yes, sports medical insurance is compulsory. It is handled by the FEDDF (the Spanish Federation of Athletes with Physical Disabilities), and we take care of your licence paperwork.
